activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted the red toy car. It sat in the middle of the shelf.

A girl stood there too. She held a blue truck. "We came to this store tomorrow," she said to her papa.

Her papa smiled. "Not tomorrow," he said. "Tomorrow comes later."

"We came yesterday," the girl said. "Yesterday already went by."

Theodore looked up at Mama. "We came today," he said. "Today is now."

"Yes," said Mama. "Now we shop."

Theodore kicked a little pebble off his shoe. It rolled under the dark shelf. The girl got down on her knees and pushed it back out to him.

The red car was still there. Mama put it in the cart. "We can pay now," she said. "We will play with it later, at home."

Theodore hugged the car all the way to the door. "Tomorrow we come again," said the girl, waving.

"Maybe tomorrow," her papa said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A scoreboard shows how many points each team has.
story:
Leon sat on the big couch at Mr. Ted's house. Everyone was watching the big game on TV. Leon could not remember who was winning.

"Papa, who has more points?" Leon asked.

"Look up high," said Papa. He pointed at the wall on the TV screen. "That is the scoreboard. It shows how many points each team has."

Leon looked. One team had a big number. One team had a small number. The team with the big number was winning.

"The red team is winning!" Leon shouted.

"Good eyes," said Mr. Ted. He bit into a cold, frozen popsicle. "Ooh, my teeth!"

Everyone laughed. Leon's shoe string had come untied, so he tied it himself.

Then the red team scored again. The scoreboard changed. The number got bigger.

"Look, look!" Leon said. "More points!"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cooks knead bread dough by pushing and folding it with their hands.
story:
Daniel was at school in the cooking classroom. He was making bread for his family. He mixed flour and water in a big bowl. Then he touched the dough. "Yuck!" said Daniel. "It's all sticky!"

The dough stuck to his fingers. It stuck to the table. "My bread is ruined," said Daniel. "It will never be bread now." His teacher smiled. "Cooks knead dough," she said. "Watch me." She pushed the dough with her hands. Then she folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold.

"Now you try," she said. Daniel pushed the dough. He folded it over. The sticky bits came off his fingers! Push and fold, push and fold. Soon the dough felt soft and smooth. "You did it!" said his teacher. Daniel laughed. "I made dough with my hands!" Later, his teacher put the bread in the oven where it was safe. Daniel waited and sniffed the air. "Mmm," he said. "Mama will smell this from home!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: In a very dark room, it is hard to tell what color things are.
story:
Luca ran to his toy box in the dark shed. He wanted his blue ball for the yard. The shed had no window. It was very dark in there. Luca grabbed a ball. "I found it!" he shouted.

He ran out to the green grass. He looked at his ball. It was not blue. It was red! Luca laughed. "The dark tricked me," he said. He ran back inside the shed. It was still dark. He felt two more balls with his hands. He could not tell which one was blue.

Then he had a big idea. He pulled the balls out into the sun. One ball was yellow. One ball was green. And there, under the bench, was his blue ball! Luca kicked it high. It bounced on the grass by the yellow flowers. "Best ball ever," said Luca. "Best day ever, too."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument.
story:
Wesley ran into the band room. He wanted to play the big violin today. He picked it up and held it upside down. He plucked the strings. He swung his arm. The violin made a sad, wobbly sound. "That is not right," said Wesley.

The music teacher came over. She smiled. "A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument," she said. She turned the violin around. She put it under Wesley's chin. She placed the bow in his little hand. Wesley pulled the bow across the strings. The violin sang out loud and sweet.

Wesley laughed. "It likes being right side up!" he said. He played again and again. His mom peeked in the door. "Is that my big boy?" she asked. Wesley played one more note. Then he took a crunchy cracker from his pocket and grinned. "I can play now, Mom!"

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Tracing around the bottom of a round cup draws a circle.
story:
John sat at the art table. He wanted to draw a sun. He tried to draw a circle. His circle came out wobbly. It went up, then down, then up again.

"You can use my cup," said Mia. She pushed her cup to him. John put the cup down on his paper. He held it with one finger on top. He traced his crayon all around the bottom of the cup. He lifted the cup up. There it was. A round circle, nice and neat.

"It's a circle!" said John. He traced it again and again. Around the circle he drew triangle rays for the sun. Then he drew a square house and a rectangle door.

"Look what the cup did," said John. Mia smiled and traced her own circle. "The cup helps," she said. The sun had a curly smile at last.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a cloudy day, clouds can hide the sun.
story:
Myles ran to the backyard with his hat. "Today I will wear my sun hat!" he said. The sun felt warm on his nose. Then a big cloud came. Where did the sun go? The cloud hid it! Now the yard felt cold. Myles shivered. "Mom, the sun is gone!"

Mom brought his sweater. "Clouds can hide the sun," she said. "But wait. It may peek back out." So Myles waited by the fence. The wind blew. His naughty hat tried to fly away! He held it tight.

"What is that?" asked Myles. A turtle sat by the rocks. It was cold too. It did not move at all. "Is the turtle going to freeze?" Mom said no. "It just likes warm sun, like you."

Then the cloud moved. The sun came back! The turtle stretched its legs. Myles took off his sweater. His hat stayed on. "Hello again, sun," said Myles.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Steam from a pot or kettle is hot and can burn, so stay back.
story:
Camille wants to see the bubbles in the pot. Grandma fills the pot with water. Then she sets it on the stove.

"Stay back," says Grandma. "Steam is hot. It can burn."

Camille wants to be brave. She takes one step. Then she stops. The steam is like a little white cloud. It goes up, up, up. It reaches her cheeks from far away. It feels warm, not cold like ice. Camille jumps back.

"Too hot," she says.

"Come hold my hand," says Grandma. "We can watch from here."

Camille holds on tight. She counts the bubbles. One, two, three, four. The water goes pop, pop, pop.

"Steam, bubbles, pot," says Camille.

She watches it all from her safe spot. Maybe tonight she will dream about little white clouds.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Sorting by color means putting all the things that are the same color together in one group.
story:
Madison wanted to build a rainbow in her backyard. She dumped out her big toy box. Red blocks rolled on the grass. Blue blocks too. Yellow blocks went everywhere.

"I will sort them," said Madison. She made a red pile. She made a blue pile. She made a yellow pile. All the red things sat together in one group. All the blue things sat together. All the yellow things sat together.

Then she saw a green block. It was hiding in the blue pile! "You do not go there," she said. She put it in its own green group.

A toy snake was green too. Madison held him tight. "You live with the green things," she said. She shut her toy box with a bang.

Then she lined up all the piles. Red, blue, yellow, green. "It's a rainbow snake," she whispered, and she wiggled him all the way home.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: It is okay for a big brother or sister to feel left out when a new baby arrives.
story:
Sophie sat in the car. She sat in her deep car seat. Mom sat in front. Baby Max sat next to Mom in his little seat.

"Drive slow," said Mom. "The baby is sleeping." Dad drove slow. The car went bump. Max woke up and cried. Sophie gave Max his soft bunny. Max held the bunny. Then he stopped crying. One bunny made one baby happy.

Sophie had a cookie in her bag. She wanted Mom to see it. But Mom was looking at Max. Mom kissed Max. Mom patted Max. Sophie got very quiet.

"Mom," said Sophie. "I miss you. Just me and you."

Mom turned around. "That's okay, Sophie. Big sisters can feel left out. I miss just you and me too."

"We can have snack time," said Sophie. "Just us two."

"Yes," said Mom. "After Max sleeps."

At home, Mom held Max. Dad rocked Max. Max closed his eyes. Then Sophie and Mom sat at the little table. Sophie held up her cookie. Mom had one too. One, two cookies.

"Just us," said Mom.

Sophie took a big bite and smiled.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Toys cannot really feel, but you can pretend they do.
story:
Benjamin was at daycare. He saw Mila crying by the toy shelf. Her doll had fallen on the floor. "She got hurt," Mila said. "She is sad."

Benjamin picked up the doll. He looked at its face. The doll did not cry. The doll was still and quiet. "Toys cannot really feel," said Teacher Rosa. "But you can pretend they do."

Benjamin had an idea. He held the doll close. He gave the doll a big hug. "There, there," he said softly. He patted the doll's back, just like his mom did for him. Mila stopped crying. She watched.

"Is the doll better now?" she asked. "Yes," said Benjamin. "The hug was magic." He laid the doll on a little blanket. He fed the doll a pretend apple. "Eat it all up," he said.

Mila smiled. She brought a stuffed bear. "The bear is scared," she said. "There is a big pretend mountain, and he has to climb it." Benjamin made his voice deep and brave. "I will help you, bear."

The two friends climbed the pretend mountain together, step by step, across the soft blue rug. "We made it to the top!" Benjamin shouted. The bear and the doll sat side by side, looking down at the whole daycare room.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Some families sing their blessing instead of speaking it.
story:
Aurora hurried into Grandma's kitchen. The whole family was there. Cousins, aunts, uncles, everyone! Big pots sat on the stove. Uncle Ben stirred them with a long spoon.

"Time for the blessing," said Grandma. "We sing it before we eat."

Aurora blinked. Sing it? She thought blessings were spoken. "Can I lead it?" she asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "You are lucky. It is your turn."

Aurora stood up tall. She took a big breath. Then she sang. But the tune came out wiggly and wrong. It sounded like a sleepy old cat. The little cousins giggled.

Aurora's face went hot. She wanted to hide under the table. But Grandma smiled and held her hand.

"Try again," said Grandma. "Slowly this time."

Aurora picked up a pencil from the counter. Grandma had drawn little notes on paper. Aurora looked at the notes. Then she sang again. She sang slowly. She sang each note in order.

This time the tune came out right. One note, then the next. The whole family joined in. Their voices filled the kitchen. Even baby cousin Sam hummed along.

When the song ended, Grandpa clapped. "That was the best one yet," he said.

"Tomorrow you can lead it again," said Grandma.

"I want to sing it twice!" said Aurora.

Grandma laughed and handed her the pencil. "We will sing it twice, and you can hold the notes."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many celebrations use candles or lamps, and grown-ups light and handle the flames.
story:
Violet walked into the big house with her mama. There were little lamps everywhere. They looked like tiny stars.

"I want to light one," said Violet. Mama held her hand. "Flames are for grown-ups," said Mama. "But you can pick which lamp I light."

Violet looked and looked. She picked a small blue lamp on a low shelf. Mama took a match and lit it. The little flame came up. It was warm and bright. Violet watched from her step back.

There was a plant in the corner with big green leaves. Shadows from the lamps danced on the plant. One shadow looked like a bear. "Is it scary?" asked Violet. "No, it is just a leaf shadow," said Mama.

Violet picked more lamps for Mama to light. "This one, and this one," she said. Mama lit each one. Soon the whole room glowed. More lamps made more light.

Grandma came over and smiled. "You chose well," she said. Violet stood very still and watched the flames. "Our house shines," she whispered. Mama gave her a soft hug. Then Violet pointed at one more lamp, a red one, way up high. "That one too," she said.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: In hide-and-seek, the seeker counts while the others hide.
story:
Violet ran to school after breakfast. She was not late today. It was playtime in the yard.

"Let's play hide-and-seek," said her friend Mia. "You seek first, Violet."

Violet put her hands on the tree. She began to count. "One, two, three, four, five!" She counted very fast. Then she turned around.

Mia was still standing in the open. Ben was half behind a bush. Nobody was hidden yet.

"You counted too fast," said Mia. "Count slowly, Violet. We need time to hide."

Violet put her hands back on the tree. "One, two, three." She went slowly now. "Four, five, six." She heard little feet running. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

She turned around. The yard was quiet. Mia was not in the open. Ben was not half behind the bush. Violet looked behind the slide. No one. She looked by the sand. Then she saw two shoes under the coats on the fence.

"Found you, Mia!" said Violet. Mia laughed and jumped out.

"You counted slow," said Mia. "Now I got to hide."

Violet smiled. "Your turn to seek," she said. "I will count to ten for you."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Day and night are opposites.
story:
Clara got to school in the dark. She thought it was morning. "Time for juice!" she said. Her teacher smiled. "Look outside, Clara," she said. Clara looked. The sky was black. One star. Two stars. Three stars. "It is still night," said her teacher. "Night and day are opposites."

Clara hung up her big coat. Her friend Sam had a small coat. Outside the window, snow fell slow. A wild bird flew fast past the glass. "The bird is fast," said Clara. "The snow is slow." The bird landed and shook one wing.

Inside, the radiator was hot. Miss Ava touched it. Clara did not touch. She held her hands far away. "Hot," said Clara. Then she picked up her cold water bottle. "Cold," she said. Big and small. Hot and cold. Fast and slow. Night and day. She counted them on her fingers. Four pairs.

They waited for the sun. Clara watched the window. Slowly the sky turned pink. Then it turned blue. "Morning!" said Sam. Clara waved at the light. "Hello, day," she said.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: A very special toy can be put away before friends come over, so you don't have to share it.
story:
William loved his little red truck. It was his very special toy. At summer camp, Miss Amy said, "Truck time, friends!"

Ben reached for the truck. William grabbed it fast. Ben's face went sad. William held the truck tight.

Then William had an idea. He walked to the shelf. He put the red truck up high, where only Miss Amy could reach. "I put it away," he said. "It can wait for me."

William found a big blue truck. He held it out to Ben. "Your turn first," said William. Ben smiled a big, friendly smile. He pushed the truck across the grass. It made a loud brmm sound. Then he gave it back. "Your turn, William!"

They took turns all morning. At water play, they filled a bowl and floated leaves in it. "You pour, then I pour," said Ben.

William's hands did not grab. They waited. And waiting made the game last a long, long time.

When camp was over, Miss Amy took the red truck down from the shelf. William hugged it all the way home.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: A zipper has two sides that join together when you pull the zipper tab up.
story:
Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. Rehmat wore her red coat. The coat hung open. The big door made wind. The wind blew the coat open wider. "Oh no!" said Rehmat. Her tummy felt cold.

Mama said, "Look at the zipper. It has two sides. Pull the tab up." Rehmat looked down. She saw two sides. She saw the little tab. She pulled the tab up. The two sides joined together. Zip! The coat closed. "I did it!" said Rehmat. She jumped up and down.

A man at the bank dropped his pen. Rehmat picked it up. She gave it back. "Thank you," said the man. "Sorry it fell," he said with a smile. Rehmat smiled too.

Then Rehmat wanted to try again. She pulled the tab down. The coat opened. She pulled the tab up. Zip! The coat closed. "Zip, zip, zip," sang Rehmat. Mama laughed. "You are so fast," said Mama. The wind blew again. This time the coat stayed warm and shut. "My turn to hold your hand," said Mama.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Once two paints are mixed together, you cannot pull them apart again.
story:
Luka was at summer camp. He sat at a paint table. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. Luka knew their names now. He said them out loud, one by one.

Luka wanted to paint a big green frog. But there was no green paint. He felt shy about asking. So he tried something. He put his brush in the blue pot. Then he put it in the yellow pot. He stirred and stirred.

The paint turned green. His frog was green. But now the yellow pot was all blue inside. Luka tipped it upside down. The paint stayed mixed. He waited. He tipped it again. The yellow did not come back out.

The teacher gave him two little cups. "Keep a bit of each paint here," she said. Luka saved some yellow and some blue. Next time, he could mix green again. He painted two frogs, then three. "Look, Mother," he said at pickup time. "I made green all by myself."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Butter from the fridge is hard, and butter left out on the counter gets softer.
story:
Joshua ran into the school cooking room. Today he would make bread for his family. Miss Ana put a bowl on the big table. "First we stir," she said. Joshua stirred the soft, squishy dough. It felt like warm mud between his fingers. "Naughty dough, you keep sticking to me!" he giggled.

Then Joshua wanted butter on his bread. He opened the little fridge. The butter was hard and cold. He pushed it with his spoon. It would not spread. It just broke the bread into pieces. One piece, two pieces, three pieces. "Oh no," said Joshua.

Miss Ana smiled. She put the hard butter on the counter. "We will let it sit," she said. Joshua waited. He counted to ten. He smelled the sweet bread baking. Miss Ana touched the butter. "Try now," she said. Joshua pushed his spoon. The butter was soft! It spread over the warm bread, one swipe, two swipes, three swipes.

Joshua held up his bread. "Mama will love this!" he said. He gave the spoon one more happy stir.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: When your turn is over, you hand the toy gently to the next person.
story:
Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. A big red truck sat on the rug. Charlie wanted it right now.

Ben had the truck first. Charlie reached out to grab it. Her hand touched the truck. The wheel scratched her finger. "Ouch," she said. The truck felt bumpy and hard.

Miss Amy knelt down beside them. She held up a little timer. "Ben, when the timer rings, your turn is done," she said. Charlie sat on her leg and waited. The timer rang. Ding! Ben lifted the truck high. He almost tossed it. Then he stopped. He put it in Charlie's hands, gently, like a baby bird.

The truck was warm from Ben's hands. Charlie pushed it across the rug. Vroom! Then the timer rang again. Now it was her turn to be done. She walked to Ben. She held the truck out softly.

"Your turn," said Charlie. Ben smiled big. Then he let her push the truck one more time, together.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it.
story:
Miles sat in the car with his blanket. He was going to get his first haircut. "I like my hair," said Miles. Mom parked the car. They walked in together.

The barber put a cape on Miles. It was blue and big. Snip, snip went the scissors. A little curl fell down. It landed on the cape. The barber brushed it into his hand.

Miles watched Mom take out a small envelope. She put the curl inside. "Why?" asked Miles. Mom said, "To remember your first haircut." Miles smiled. He held the envelope all the way to the car. The curl was soft, like his blanket. Mom buckled him in. Miles looked at the envelope. "We keep it," he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Parker had a gift in his bag. It was for his mom. It was a picture he painted yesterday. Today he wanted to give it to her. But Mom would come later, after school.

"When is later?" Parker asked his teacher.

"Look at the clock," she said. "A clock shows what time it is."

The big hand pointed to the twelve. The little hand pointed to the nine. Parker watched the clock. He painted some more. He played with blocks. He helped dry the cups after snack.

Then the big hand moved. Now it pointed all the way around to the twelve again. The little hand pointed to the twelve too.

"That is twelve o'clock," said his teacher. "Time to go!"

The door opened. Mom was there. Parker ran and hugged her. "This is for you," he said. "I made it yesterday. Today I missed you."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Asking family to help look means more people are searching.
story:
Anna was at the school playground. Her bunny was gone. "Where is bunny?" she said. She looked under the slide. No bunny. She looked by the swing. No bunny. Anna sat down on the short wall. She wanted to cry.

Then her big sister came. "I can help you look," said Mia. "Two people can look." Dad came too. "Now we all can look," he said. Anna looked by the sand. Mia looked by the park gate. Dad looked in the toy box. Dad lifted a small coat. The coat was folded on top of something soft. There was bunny!

"My bunny!" said Anna. She hugged bunny tight. More people looked, and they found her. "Let's go home," said Dad, and Anna held Mia's hand all the way.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: A beanbag lands with a soft flop instead of bouncing like a ball.
story:
Milo went to the park with Dad. He saw a big red hoop on the grass. "I want to throw my ball in," said Milo. He threw his ball at the hoop. The ball hit the rim and bounced away. It rolled down the hill. Milo ran after it, but he felt dizzy from spinning around. Dad caught the ball for him.

Then Milo found a small beanbag in the toy bag. He threw the beanbag at the hoop. It did not bounce away. It hit the rim and went flop. It fell soft and slow, right into the hoop. "It went in!" said Milo. He threw the beanbag again and again. Each time it went flop, flop, right in.

Dad held out a big ball. "Now catch it with both hands," said Dad. Milo held out both arms. The ball came down and Milo caught it in a big hug. Milo laughed and laughed. The world felt sunny and good. He filled his arms with the ball and ran to Dad for one more throw.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: When a grown-up reads a book aloud, they are reading the words, not just looking at the pictures.
story:
Eli wanted a story about a big red truck. He could not find one at daycare. He looked in the little basket. He looked under the rug. Then he found a book with a truck on the top.

Eeli sat down with the book. He opened it from the back. Miss Ana came over. "Books start at the front," she said. She turned the book around. "We read from here." She pointed to the first page. Then she put her finger under the little black marks. "These are words," she said. "I read the words out loud." She read them, and the story came out!

Eli turned a page. There were no words there, just a picture of the truck going fast. "Read this one!" he said. Miss Ana smiled. "There are no words on this page," she said. "There is nothing written here to read." So they just looked at the picture together.

Eli got another book. He opened it at the front. He put his finger under the words. "Read these!" he said. Miss Ana read them all. Eli clapped. At pickup time, he ran to his dad. "Dad, read the words!" he said, holding up the book.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cake batter is runny when it goes into the oven and comes out as a cake you can slice.
story:
Today was Daddy's birthday. Lena wanted to make him a cake. She helped Mama crack the eggs. The batter dripped off the spoon. Lena frowned. "It is so runny!" she said. "It will spill all over. It can't be a cake." Mama smiled. "Watch the oven," she said. Mama poured the batter into a pan. Then Mama put the pan in the oven. Lena stood back, far from the hot door. She waited. She wiggled her toes. "Is it still runny in there?" she asked. Mama said, "You will see."

The kitchen got warm. A sweet smell filled the room. Lena sniffed and sniffed. The timer rang and she gave a little yell. Mama put on big mitts. She pulled out a real cake. It was tall and golden. Lena poked it with one finger. It was soft, but not runny at all. "Mama, look!" she said. "It got thick!" Mama cut one slice for Daddy. Lena drew a fox on his card. Daddy took a big bite. "Best cake ever," he said. "Lena made it!" Lena grinned and clapped her hands.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, lion dancers move to the beat of loud drums.
story:
Lillian went to the cultural center with Mama and Baba. Red paper lanterns hung from the ceiling. Lillian wanted to see the lion dance.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! They were so noisy. Lillian hid behind Mama's back. The big lion came out. It was red and gold. But the lion did not move.

Mama held her hand. "Look at the lion," she said. "Listen to the drums." The drummer hit the drum. Boom! Then the lion jumped. The drummer hit it again. Boom! Then the lion shook its head. Lillian saw it. The drums made the lion dance!

She came out from behind Mama. She clapped her hands to the beat. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! The lion hopped to her. It blinked its big eyes. Lillian laughed and clapped some more.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: In busy places like airports, children stay close to their grown-up and hold hands.
story:
Henry buckled his seat in the car. "Are we going far away?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "We are going on a plane!" Henry bounced in his seat. He looked out the window the whole way. The clouds looked big and stormy, but the sky near the airport was blue.

At the airport, Henry saw the planes. They were huge! He wanted to run to the window. But there were so many people. Mom held out her hand. "In busy places like airports, children stay close to their grown-up and hold hands," she said. Henry grabbed her hand tight.

They walked and walked. Henry saw a man with a big shoe in his bag. He saw a little girl with her dad. She was holding his hand too. Then Henry saw it. A big plane went up, up, up into the sky! The plane made wind. The wind pushed a hat right off a man's head. The hat flew and landed on the ground. The man laughed and picked it up.

"That was so big!" said Henry. "Can we fly next?" "Yes," said Dad. "It is our turn now." Henry held Mom's hand all the way to the door of the plane. Then he climbed the steps, one at a time, still holding on.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a snowy day, mittens or gloves keep your hands warm.
story: Ibrahim looked out the window. White flakes fell from the sky. "It is snowy today," said Mama. "Snowy!" said Ibrahim. He put on his boots. He put on his puffy coat. He ran outside and made a snowball. His hands felt cold. Very cold. "Ow," said Ibrahim. He ran back to Mama. "Hands are cold!" Mama held his little red hands. "Your mittens," she said. "Mittens keep your hands warm." Ibrahim remembered his mittens. They were on the shelf by the door. He pulled them on. His hands felt warm. Good and warm. He made a new snowball. He threw it at the fence. Then he heard a beep. His toy robot sat in the snow by the door. "Robot is outside!" said Ibrahim. He picked the robot up with his warm mittens and hugged it all the way inside.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: Rhyming words end with the same sound, like cat and hat.
story:
Evelyn lived in a red brick house with Mama. Mama put on a song. It had a steady beat. Evelyn stomped her feet. She stomped too fast. She got all mixed up.

"Try clapping," said Mama. Mama clapped slowly. Clap, clap, clap. Evelyn watched Mama's hands. Then she clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps fit the beat. Her blocks on the floor bounced a little with each clap. "My blocks are dancing!" said Evelyn.

Then Mama sang a rhyme. "The cat sat on his mat, and he wore a big..." Mama stopped. Evelyn knew this one. She forgot the last word. She thought hard. "Cat, mat, hat!" said Evelyn. "Hat!" It fit. Cat and hat and mat all ended the same. "Yes, the big hat," laughed Mama. Evelyn sang it again by herself. She did not forget the hat this time.

Evelyn stood on her little stool. She clapped the beat and sang the whole rhyme. Clap, clap, clap. "The cat sat on his mat, and he wore a big hat!" Her red block bounced on the floor. "Again!" said Evelyn. Mama pressed play.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: People say 'thank you' after someone gives them something or helps them.
story:
Kinsley went to the park with her dad. She saw a boy named Sam by the sandbox. Sam had a big red ball. Kinsley wanted to play with it. She walked over to Sam. "Can I have the ball, please?" she asked. Sam passed the ball to her. It was slippery and Kinsley dropped it. "Sorry," she said. Sam smiled and picked it up.

Then Sam's friend Max ran by. Max took the ball and ran off with it. Kinsley felt sad. But Max turned back. "Thank you, Sam!" he called. Sam waved. Kinsley saw that. People say thank you when someone gives them something.

Dad sat on the square bench nearby. Kinsley could not reach the swing. "Dad, can you help me, please?" she asked. Dad lifted her up. "Thank you," said Kinsley. She swung high and laughed. Then she and Sam rolled the red ball on the grass. "Thank you for playing," said Sam. "You too!" said Kinsley.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: At an animal shelter, pets wait for a family to adopt them and take them home.
story:
Paisley held Mama's hand at the shelter. Cats and dogs sat in little rooms with doors. "They wait here," said Mama. "They wait for a family to take them home."

Paisley walked past the dogs. She walked past the cats. Then she saw a small gray cat. The cat looked back at her. "This one," said Paisley. "This one waits for me."

A helper opened the door. The cat rode home in a box with holes. At home, Paisley set out water. She set out food. "Kittens get scared," said Mama. "Let's be quiet." Paisley sat very still on the floor.

The moon came up. The cat peeked out of the box. It sniffed the water. It drank a little sip. Paisley saw the water go down in the bowl. She put a bit more in. The cat drank again. "You were thirsty," whispered Paisley. The cat curled up next to her. Paisley petted its soft fur, very, very gently.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: Your skin can feel whether something is soft or rough.
story:
Georgia put on her big farm hat. The hat was too loose. It fell over her eyes. "I want to help," she said.

Farmer Ben smiled. "You can sort this basket," he said. "Find the soft things. Find the rough things." Georgia touched a feather. It tickled her hand. "Soft," she said. She touched a pinecone. It was bumpy and hard on her fingers. "Rough," she said. Then she touched a soft blanket. Her hand felt the softness right away.

"My hand knows!" said Georgia. "My skin tells me soft or rough." Farmer Ben nodded. "Yes, your skin feels it," he said. Georgia touched the baby chick's fluffy feathers. Soft. She touched the old wooden fence. Rough. She laughed and clapped.

Then Georgia found a smooth stone. It was not soft like the feather. It was not rough like the pinecone. "This one is in the middle," she said. She put the stone in her pocket. She ran to show her mama. "Feel this!" said Georgia. "My skin can tell!"

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Pulling the zipper tab down opens your coat.
story:
Olivia stood by the little clock at school. It was time to go outside. Miss Ana held up Olivia's coat. "Can you try?" she asked.

Olivia pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat sat on her shoulders. Now the zipper. She pinched the tab and pushed it up. It would not go. It slid down instead. The coat opened wide. "Look," said Olivia. "Down makes it open." She tried again. She pushed the tab up, slowly, slowly. Zip! The coat was closed.

At recess, Olivia ran and jumped. She got very warm. So she pulled the tab down. The coat opened all by itself. Cool air came in. "I did it," she said. Her friend Ben wore a different coat. His zipper went down too. After play, Miss Ana said it was almost time to wash hands, like a little bath for fingers. Olivia zipped her coat up again. "All done," she said.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The word 'five' and the numeral 5 mean the same number.
story:
Axel sat down at the dinner table. He saw a card by his plate. The card had a big shape on it. "What is that?" he asked. "That is a five," said Mom. "It is the same five you count. One, two, three, four, five." Axel looked at his hand. He tapped his fingers. One, two, three, four, five. "The five on the card is my five fingers!" he said.

"Tonight you get five green beans," said Mom. She put beans on his plate. Axel counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." But then he ate one fast. Now he saw four beans. One bean was missing. "I ate too fast," he said. "I forget to save them."

Dad held up his plate. "Want to count mine?" he asked. Axel pointed at each bean. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad laughed. "Ten beans. That is a lot." Axel tapped his ten fingers too. "Ten fingers, ten beans," he said.

Then Dad slid two beans over. "For you," he said. Axel counted his beans again. "Four, five, six, seven. Seven!" He pushed his card so the big five could see. "Look, five," he said. "Seven is more than you." Then he picked up a bean and grinned.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Now means at this very moment.
story:
Milan loved story time at school. He wanted a story now. He ran to Teacher Rosa.

"Can we have the story now?" he asked.

Teacher Rosa smiled. "Not now. Now means at this very moment. First we have snack. The story comes later."

Milan sat down. He looked at the clock. He ate his crackers. He drank his water. He waited and waited.

"Now?" he asked again.

"Not yet," said Teacher Rosa. "Now you are eating. Later we will cook pretend soup in the story."

Milan kept waiting. He stacked a coin on the table. He watched the bright fish swim in the tank. He waited some more.

Yesterday the story was about a red bus. Today the story would be about soup. Tomorrow there would be a new story too.

At last Teacher Rosa clapped her hands. "Snack is done. The story is now!"

Milan jumped up. "Now, now, now!" he said.

He sat on the rug and hugged his knees. "Once there was a big pot," Teacher Rosa began.

Milan leaned in close to hear.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
story:
Jaxson was playing in the yard. He dug in the dirt with his little shovel. His hands got dirty. His sister, a big girl named Mia, called him in for lunch.

Jaxson ran to the table. He saw bread, cheese, and apple slices. He counted them out loud. One apple, two apples, three apples. He reached for his plate.

Mia held up her hand. "Stop. Look at your hands." Jaxson looked. There was dirt on his fingers. Mia pointed to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Jaxson walked to the sink. Mia turned on the water. It felt warm and bubbly. The soap smelled like lemons. Jaxson rubbed his hands together. The bubbles took the dirt away. He rinsed and dried them on the soft towel.

Then he sat down and picked up his apple slice. It was clean and sweet. Jaxson smiled. "Wash first, then eat," he said. Mia laughed and gave him a kiss on his head. After lunch, Jaxson yawned and whispered, "Bath next."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Taking photos on a trip lets a family remember it after they get home.
story:
Zoe went to the park with Mama and Dad. The park had big trees and a lake. "Look, a deer!" said Dad. Zoe waved at the deer. It ran away.

Zoe found a pretty rock by the water. It was gray with white lines. She put it in her pocket. Then Zoe saw a big wheel on a car. It was parked in the mud. The wheel spun and spun. Mud went splat on the grass. "The wheel made the mud fly!" said Zoe.

Dad opened his backpack. He took out a camera. "Smile, Zoe," he said. Click! He took a photo of Zoe and the rock. Click! He took a photo of the deer track in the mud. Zoe helped Dad find more things to snap. A tall tree. A red bird. The lake.

At home, Zoe felt sad. "I miss the park," she said. Mama opened the photo book. There was Zoe with her rock. There was the tall tree and the red bird. "We can look any time we want," said Mama. Zoe held her gray rock tight. "Again," she said. "Show the deer track again."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Billie stood in the kitchen. The pot on the stove went puff, puff, puff. "Hot," said Mom. "Stay back." Billie stayed back. She touched the cold milk carton instead. It felt smooth and cool.

Then Mom said, "We need apples. Let's go to the store." The store was big and bright. The doors went swing, and in they walked. Billie held Mom's hand. But then she saw a red swing toy on a shelf, and she stopped to look. When she looked up, Mom was gone. Billie asked herself, "What do I do now?" She knew the answer. Find a store worker. She saw a woman at the checkout with a green vest. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. The woman smiled and took her hand. Mom came running, and Billie hugged her tight. "Let's get those apples," said Mom.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.
story:
Hayden wants to wash his hands. He stands by the sink. Mom turns the tap. First the water runs cold. Then it runs warm. Mom checks it with her hand. "Just right," she says.

On the shelf, Hayden sees something. Little red dots in a bottle. They look like candy. He wants one. He reaches up high. "Wait," says Mom. She puts her hand out. Hayden stops.

"Those are not candy," says Mom. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." She takes the bottle down. She clicks the cap shut. She puts the bottle up high, far away.

"Can I wash my lion now?" asks Hayden. He holds up his special toy lion. Mom laughs. "Yes. Hold him up to the water." Hayden holds the lion under the tap. Cold water runs over the lion's paws. Hayden laughs too.

Mom dries the lion with a soft towel. Hayden hugs him tight. "All clean," he says.
